1. The present accident claim is based on a detailed accident report (Dar) filed by the police in
terms of provisions of Mv Act. 
2.  The brief facts of the case are that on 24.01.2020, petitioner Teena Yadav aged about 18 years was going towards her home, riding a Scooty bearing no. RJ-14WD-8813 with her cousins brothers Nirbhay(aged7years) and Ranveer(aged 9 years) after picking them from school. At about 1 pm,
when she was on 3rd Avenue Road at the first crossing, near Block-13, a Pulse Renault car bearing no. DL-1OQ-5860(hereinafter referred to as offending vehicle) came from her left side, driven in a rash and negligent manner and at a high speed and hit the Scooty which the petitioner was riding. 
As a result all three of them fell from the Scooty and sustained injuries. Driver of the offending vehicle took the injured persons including the petitioner to the hospital. 
3. An FIR no.0024 dated 24.01.2020 was registered u/s 279,337 of IPC at PS Lodhi Colony and the matter was investigated. After investigation, a charge sheet was filed before concerned criminal court against the driver of the offending vehicle(Respondent no.1) while DAR was filed before this Tribunal. 17:05:10 +0530 MACT NO:783/21 Teena v. Arun Kumar P.No. 2 Of 18 BK 4. Respondent no.1 is driver, Respondent no.2 is owner of the offending vehicle and Respondent no.3 is the insurance company with which the offending vehicle was insured. 
5. In response to the DAR, Respondent no. 1 and 2 filed their reply denying their fault or liability. It is denied that the accident took place due to rash and negligent driving by Respondent no.1. It has been pleaded that in fact the petitioner namely Teena Yadav was triple riding with the other two injured persons, without having a valid driving licence and without the Scooty that she was riding being duly insured. It is therefore that petitioner Teena Yadav was also convicted u/s 3/181,196 &
128/177 of M.V. Act in a kalandra dated 24.11.2021. It has been pleaded that the petitioner was not only driving the Scooty rashly and negligently and at a very high speed but was also grossly negligent in so far as she was riding two minor children on her Scooty and therefore is solely liable to compensate the other injured. It is further pleaded that even the offending vehicle is duly insured. 
As per reply filed by insurance company, liability is denied on the ground of negligence of the petitioner apparent from the fact that she was triple riding on a Scooty without holding a valid driving licence or wearing helmet. It has been pleaded that since petitioner has also been challaned u/s 128/177 & 129/177 MV Act, she is not entitled to compensation. It is further pleaded that the case is bad for misjoinder and non-joinder of proper parties. 
6. After completion of pleadings, following issues were framed on 10.03.2022.

2. Whether the injured is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom? OPP.

7. To prove her claim, petitioner led her evidence by examining herself as PW-1 by way of affidavit as Ex.PW-1/1. As per the affidavit, on 24.01.2020 at about 1.00 PM, she alongwith her cousin brothers was returning back after picking them from school. When she reached at 3rd Avenue Road, Block No.13, offending vehicle bearing no. DL-1CQ-5860, a silver colour pulse Renault came from right side with over speed and hit her Scooty bearing no. RJ-14-WD-8813, as a result she fell down and received injuries. She was 18 years of age at the time of accident. She deposed that she spent Rs.25,000/- on her treatment and special diet. She relied upon DAR as Ex.PW-1/A She was duly cross-examined by learned counsel for insurance company. 
No evidence has been led on behalf of the respondents. 
8. Final arguments in details were addressed on behalf of the claimant/injured and the insurance company. On the basis of pleadings of the parties, evidence adduced and arguments addressed,
issue wise findings are as under:
Whether the injured suffered injuries in a road traffic accident on 24.01.2020 due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle no. DL-1CP-5860 being driven by R1, owned by R2and insured with R3? OPP. Digitally signed by CHARU CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date:
2024.11.21 17:06:22 +0530 MACT NO:783/21 Teena v. Arun Kumar P.No. 4 Of 18 BK 9. Before proceeding to decide the above issue, it is apposite to note that as a settled principle of law,
proceedings under The Motor Vehicle Act are not considered akin to the proceedings in a civil suit and hence strict rules of evidence are not applicable. Reliance is placed upon decision in Bimla Devi & ors. vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Ors. (2009) 13 SC 535, in Parmeshwari vs. Amir Chand & Ors., 2011 (1) SCR 1096 and National Insurance Company Ltd. vs. Pushpa Rana, 2009 ACJ 287, wherein it has been held that the negligence has to be decided on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities and a holistic view has to be taken. 
10. In the instant case, petitioner Teena Yadav has testified the date as well as the manner of accident. During her cross- examination,however, she has admitted that at the time of accident she was not holding any driving licence. She denied her knowledge if the Scooty that she was riding was having any valid insurance cover. She further admitted that she was triple riding with injured Nirbhay Yadav and Ranvir Yadav(both minors). She also conceded that Nirbhay and Ranvir/pillion Teena (Dar) vs Arun Kumar(24/20Lc) on 21 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/185459878/
3 riders were not wearing any helmet. Further, it is a matter of record that petitioner Teena Yadav was convicted in kalandra for the offence of triple riding, without a driving licence. It is pertinent to note that the Ld. counsel for insurance company as well as Ld. counsel for driver and owner have pleaded that the accident occurred due to sole negligence of petitioner Teena Nagpal and for this purpose have strongly relied upon her cross-examination where PW Teena Yadav has identified the site plan showing that the accident occurred in the middle of a four way crossing. She CHARU by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date: 2024.11.21 17:06:32 +0530 MACT NO:783/21 Teena v. Arun Kumar P.No. 5 Of 18 BK conceded that at the time of driving of Scooty she did not slow down her Scooty and maintained a speed of 20-30 km. per hour. She also stated that at the time of accident she was talking to her cousins who were sitting behind her on the said Scooty. This court has perused the site plan which confirms that the accident occurred in the middle of the crossing where no traffic light was installed. As such, though petitioner's conduct contributed to the accident in as much as she did not possess a driving licence and was driving with two more pillion riders, both minors at a crossing without ensuring extra caution particularly as there was no traffic light, she cannot be said to be solely responsible for the accident as the offending vehicle also ought to have been extra careful in driving through the crossing. Had the offending vehicle also maintained a slow speed as that of the Scooty which the petitioner was driving, the accident could have possibly been averted. The presence of fresh damage marks on the offending vehicle, as seen in the mechanical inspection report rules out the possibility of non-occurrence of the collision between these two vehicles. 
As such, considering that the petitioner was without a driving licence and triple riding a Scooty with two minor children, a deduction of at least 50% is liable to be made from the compensation towards contributory negligence. 
11. In totality of circumstances, this Tribunal is of the opinion that the petitioner has been able to prove on the scales of preponderance of probabilities that the accident in question took place due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle by its driver/respondent no.1 on the date and time of accident CHARU Digitally signed by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date: 2024.11.21 17:06:45 +0530 MACT NO:783/21 Teena v. Arun Kumar P.No. 6 Of 18 BK while respondents have also proved contributory negligence on the part of the petitioner. Issue no.1 is accordingly decided. 
Issue no. 2 Whether the injured is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom? OPP.
12. No statutory defence has been raised by the insurance company. As such, insurance company is liable to compensate the petitioner. 
13. As regards the quantum of compensation, this court is governed by the law laid down by Hon'le Supreme Court in Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr. (2011) 1 Supreme Court cases 343, Sarla Verma & Ors. v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Ors. (2003) 6SCC 121 and National Insurance Company Limited v. Pranay Sethi & Ors.(2017) 16 SCC 680. The gist of the law is that the object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner. The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with Teena (Dar) vs Arun Kumar(24/20Lc) on 21 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/185459878/
4 reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable. A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury. 
This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have CHARU by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA 2024.11.21 Date:
17:06:56 +0530 MACT NO:783/21 Teena v. Arun Kumar P.No. 7 Of 18 BK earned.
14. Further it can be noted that the heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary damages (Special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability. 
(iii) Future medical expenses. Non-pecuniary damages (General damages) 
(iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries. 
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage). 
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
14.1. In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii) (a)
and (iv). 14.2. It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii)(b), (iii),
(v) and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities CHARU Digitally signed by CHARU GUPTA Date: 2024.11.21 GUPTA 17:07:06 +0530 MACT NO:783/21 Teena v. Arun Kumar P.No. 8 Of 18 BK (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life. 
14.3. Assessment of pecuniary damages under Item (i) and under Item (ii) (a) do not pose much difficulty as they involve reimbursement of actuals and are easily ascertainable from the evidence.

5 14.4. Award under the head of future medical expenses--Item (iii)--depends upon specific medical evidence regarding need for further treatment and cost thereof. 
14.5. Assessment of non-pecuniary damages--Items (iv), (v) and (vi)--involves determination of l u m p s u m a m o u n t s w i t h r e f e r e n c e t o c i r c u m s t a n c e s s u c h a s a g e , n a t u r e o f injury/deprivation/disability suffered by the claimant and the effect thereof on the future life of the claimant. Decisions of Hon'ble SC and Hon'ble High Courts contain necessary guidelines for award under these heads, if necessary. 14.6. It was observed by Hon'ble Sc in such case of Raj Kumar (supra) that what usually poses some difficulty is the assessment of the loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability --Item (ii) (a).
14.7. We are not concerned with assessment regarding loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability in this case, as petitioner did not suffer any permanent disability. 
15. Though no age proof of the petitioner has been filed, her age has been disclosed as 18 years in the medical documents. Further, though the petitioner has claimed to be earning, no proof of employment, salary or income has been filed. 
As per MLC of the injured prepared at Jai Prakash Narain Digitally signed CHARU by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date: 2024.11.21 17:07:17 +0530 MACT NO:783/21 Teena v. Arun Kumar P.No. 9 Of 18 BK Apex Trauma Center and discharge note, petitioner suffered abrasion over lower and upper lip, right iliac region and left lateral malleolus. Thus, the injuries suffered by petitioner is simple. She did not undergo any hospitalization. Thus, keeping in view the nature of injuries,
petitioner cannot be said to have suffered any loss of income on account of injury sustained in the accident. 
16. Further, petitioner has not filed medical bills and has been treated in a government hospital. 
Thus, there has been no medical expenditure for treatment incurred by her. As such, no compensation can be granted under this head. She has admitted to have been taken to the hospital by Respondent no.1 himself and as such did not incur any expenditure on the conveyance. 
17. No compensation towards future loss of income can be granted in cases where petitioner has not proved to have sustained any permanent disability.

22. Another issue which is to be decided is out of such Award amount, how much is to be released at present and how much is to kept in the form of FDR for future financial used of the petitioner. 
23. At this stage, it is relevant to the refer to the judgment of A. V. Padma & Ors. Vs., R. Venugopal &
Ors. (2012) 3 Supreme Court Cases 378:
"...... In the case of Susamma Thomas (supra), this Court issued certain guidelines in order to "safeguard the feed from being frittered away by the beneficiaries due to ignorance, illiteracy and susceptibility to exploitation". 
Even as per the guidelines issued by this Court Court, long term fixed deposit of amount of compensation is mandatory only in the case of minors, illiterate claimants and widows. In the case of illiterate claimants, the Tribunal is allowed to consider the request for lumpsum payment for effecting purchase of any movable property such as agricultural implements, rickshaws etc. to earn a living. However, in such cases, the Tribunal shall Digitally signed CHARU by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date: 2024.11.21 17:08:30 +0530 MACT NO:783/21 Teena v. Arun Kumar P.No. 14 Of 18 BK make sure that the amount is actually spent for the purpose and the demand is not a ruse to Teena (Dar) vs Arun Kumar(24/20Lc) on 21 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/185459878/
9 withdraw money. In the case of semi-illiterate claimants, the Tribunal should ordinarily invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit. But if the Tribunal is satisfied for reasons to be stated in writing that the whole or part of the amount is required for expanding an existing business or for purchasing some property for earning a livelihood, the Tribunal can release the whole or part of the amount of compensation to the claimant provided the Tribunal will ensure that the amount is invested for the purpose for which it is demanded and paid. In the case of literate persons, it is not mandatory to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit. 
The expression used in guideline No. (iv) issued by this Court is that in the case of literate persons also the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No. (i), whereas in the guideline Nos.
(i), (ii), (iii) and (v), the expression used is that the Tribunal should. Moreover, in the case of literate persons, the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No. (i) only if, having regard to the age, fiscal background and strata of the society to which the claimant belongs and such other considerations, the Tribunal thinks that in the larger interest of the claimant and with a view to ensure the safety of the compensation awarded, it is necessary to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit. 
Thus, sufficient discretion has been given to the Tribunal not to insist on investment of the compensation amount in long term fixed deposit and to release even the whole amount in the case of literate persons. However, the Tribunals are often taking a very rigid stand and are mechanically ordering in almost all cases that the amount of compensation shall be invested in long term fixed deposit. They are taking such a rigid and CHARU Digitally signed by CHARU GUPTA MACT NO:783/21 Teena v. Arun Kumar GUPTA Date: 2024.11.21 17:09:23 +0530 P.No. 15 Of 18 BK mechanical approach without understanding and appreciating the distinction drawn by this Court in the case of minors, illiterate claimants and widows and in the case of semiliterate and literate persons. It needs to be clarified that the above guidelines were issued by this Court only to safeguard the interests of the claimants, particularly the minors, illiterates and others whose amounts are sought to be withdrawn on some fictitious grounds. The guidelines were not to be understood to mean that the Tribunals were to take a rigid stand while considering an application seeking release of the money. 
The guidelines cast a responsibility on the Tribunals to pass appropriate orders after examining each case on its own merits. However, it is seen that even in cases when there is no possibility or chance of the feed being frittered away by the beneficiary owing to ignorance, illiteracy or susceptibility to exploitation, investment of the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit is directed by the Tribunals as a matter of course and in a routine manner, ignoring the object and the spirit of the guidelines issued by this Court and the genuine requirements of the claimants. Even in the case of literate persons, the Tribunals are automatically ordering investment of the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit without recording that having regard to the age or fiscal background or the strata of the society to which the claimant belongs or such other considerations,
the Tribunal thinks it necessary to direct such investment in the larger interests of the claimant and with a view to ensure the safety of the compensation awarded to him.

Further it can be noted that the heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary damages (Special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:

(iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.

(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage).

summary.ANALYSIS:
Before proceeding to decide the above issue, it is apposite to note that as a settled principle of law,
proceedings under The Motor Vehicle Act are not considered akin to the proceedings in a civil suit and hence strict rules of evidence are not applicable.
As such, though petitioner's conduct contributed to the accident in as much as she did not possess a driving licence and was driving with two more pillion riders, both minors at a crossing without ensuring extra caution particularly as there was no traffic light, she cannot be said to be solely responsible for the accident as the offending vehicle also ought to have been extra careful in driving through the crossing.
The presence of fresh damage marks on the offending vehicle, as seen in the mechanical inspection report rules out the possibility of non-occurrence of the collision between these two vehicles.

As such, considering that the petitioner was without a driving licence and triple riding a Scooty with two minor children, a deduction of at least 50% is liable to be made from the compensation towards contributory negligence.

13. As regards the quantum of compensation, this court is governed by the law laid down by Hon'le Supreme Court in Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr. (2011) 1 Supreme Court cases 343, Sarla Verma & Ors. v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Ors. (2003) 6SCC 121 and National Insurance Company Limited v. Pranay Sethi & Ors.(2017) 16 SCC 680.
She did not undergo any hospitalization.
Thus, keeping in view the nature of injuries,
petitioner cannot be said to have suffered any loss of income on account of injury sustained in the accident.
16. Further, petitioner has not filed medical bills and has been treated in a government hospital.

Thus, there has been no medical expenditure for treatment incurred by her.

17. No compensation towards future loss of income can be granted in cases where petitioner has not proved to have sustained any permanent disability.
In the case of semi-illiterate claimants, the Tribunal should ordinarily invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit.
But if the Tribunal is satisfied for reasons to be stated in writing that the whole or part of the amount is required for expanding an existing business or for purchasing some property for earning a livelihood, the Tribunal can release the whole or part of the amount of compensation to the claimant provided the Tribunal will ensure that the amount is invested for the purpose for which it is demanded and paid.
In the case of literate persons, it is not mandatory to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit.

The expression used in guideline No. (iv) issued by this Court is that in the case of literate persons also the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No. (i), whereas in the guideline Nos.
(i), (ii), (iii) and (v), the expression used is that the Tribunal should.
Moreover, in the case of literate persons, the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No. (i) only if, having regard to the age, fiscal background and strata of the society to which the claimant belongs and such other considerations, the Tribunal thinks that in the larger interest of the claimant and with a view to ensure the safety of the compensation awarded, it is necessary to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit.

Thus, sufficient discretion has been given to the Tribunal not to insist on investment of the compensation amount in long term fixed deposit and to release even the whole amount in the case of literate persons.
However, the Tribunals are often taking a very rigid stand and are mechanically ordering in almost all cases that the amount of compensation shall be invested in long term fixed deposit.
However, it is seen that even in cases when there is no possibility or chance of the feed being frittered away by the beneficiary owing to ignorance, illiteracy or susceptibility to exploitation, investment of the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit is directed by the Tribunals as a matter of course and in a routine manner, ignoring the object and the spirit of the guidelines issued by this Court and the genuine requirements of the claimants.
Even in the case of literate persons, the Tribunals are automatically ordering investment of the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit without recording that having regard to the age or fiscal background or the strata of the society to which the claimant belongs or such other considerations,
the Tribunal thinks it necessary to direct such investment in the larger interests of the claimant and with a view to ensure the safety of the compensation awarded to him.
